Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) syndromes are inherited disorders characterized by tumors in multiple endocrine glands, with MEN1, MEN2A, and MEN2B being key examples.

This document provides comprehensive MBChB-level revision notes on endocrine pathology, covering disorders of the pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal glands, and pancreas, as well as multiple endocrine neoplasia syndromes.
It also details the genetic basis and clinical manifestations of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) syndromes, alongside a comparison of parathyroid cell types.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) are inherited syndromes causing tumors in two or more endocrine organs. Three main types (MEN1, MEN2A, MEN2B) have distinct genetic mutations and clinical patterns.

sections.p: MEN syndromes are autosomal‑dominant disorders defined by the presence of tumors in at least two endocrine glands, confirmed by genetic testing for MEN1, RET, or CDKN1B mutations.
b: Diagnosis requires clinical criteria + pathogenic mutation
Screening of first‑degree relatives is mandatory

t.b: Does the patient carry a pathogenic mutation? Positive result confirms syndrome and guides family testing
Does the patient meet organ‑specific tumor thresholds? Meets criteria → diagnose specific MEN type

sections.p: Severity is staged by the number of glands involved, tumor size, and presence of malignancy. The American Thyroid Association (ATA) risk categories are used for medullary thyroid carcinoma in MEN2.
b: Stage I: single benign tumor
Stage II: multiple benign tumors
Stage III: any malignant tumor or metastatic disease

sections.p: MEN1 results from MEN1 gene loss; MEN2A/2B from activating RET mutations. Rarely, de novo mutations occur.
b: MEN1 gene mutation – most common cause of MEN1
RET proto‑oncogene mutation – causes MEN2A/2B
Occasional de novo RET mutation in families without history

sections.p: Patients develop hyperparathyroidism, pituitary adenomas, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (MEN1) or medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, parathyroid hyperplasia (MEN2). Symptoms reflect hormone excess or mass effect.
b: Hypercalcemia → stones, bone pain, abdominal groans
Peptic ulcer disease from gastrinoma
Hypertension, headaches from pheochromocytoma

sections.p: Targeted imaging and biochemical screens identify affected glands and functional status.

t.b: Is hyperparathyroidism present? Elevated calcium with inappropriately high PTH confirms parathyroid involvement
Is pheochromocytoma present? Elevated metanephrines indicate catecholamine‑secreting tumor
Is medullary thyroid carcinoma present? High calcitonin is highly sensitive for MTC
Are pancreatic or adrenal masses present? Imaging localises neuroendocrine tumors

t.a: If a test is unavailable (e.g., calcitonin assay)
t.b: What alternative can be used? Use neck ultrasound and fine‑needle aspiration with immunocytochemistry for calcitonin

sections.p: Malignant transformation, metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma crisis, and severe hypercalcemia are life‑threatening.
b: Sudden hypertensive emergency → pheochromocytoma crisis
Rapidly rising calcium → hypercalcemic coma
Progressive neck mass with dysphagia → invasive MTC

sections.p: Treat each tumour according to its organ, then provide lifelong surveillance. Surgery is curative for most benign lesions; targeted therapies are used for metastatic disease.
b: Parathyroidectomy for hyperparathyroidism – removes source of calcium excess
Total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection for medullary thyroid carcinoma – prevents recurrence
Adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma – eliminates catecholamine surge
Somatostatin analogues for functional pancreatic NETs – control hormone secretion
Avoid prophylactic radiation; reserve tyrosine‑kinase inhibitors for progressive metastatic MTC

sections.p: Lifelong annual biochemical screening and periodic imaging detect new tumours early. Genetic counselling reduces familial risk.
b: Annual calcium, PTH, calcitonin, and metanephrines
MRI of neck and abdomen every 2–3 years
Counselling for at‑risk relatives and cascade testing

sections.p: MEN can be mistaken for sporadic endocrine tumours or other hereditary syndromes.
b: Sporadic medullary thyroid carcinoma without RET mutation
Von Hippel‑Lindau disease (pheochromocytoma, pancreatic NETs)
Carney complex (pituitary and adrenal lesions)

sections.p: Certain labs may be falsely normal early in disease.
b: Normal calcium early in MEN1 despite parathyroid hyperplasia – repeat testing if symptoms arise
Calcitonin may be modestly elevated in chronic renal failure – correlate with imaging

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe hypertension or headache (pheochromocytoma crisis)
Confusion, polyuria, or renal failure from hypercalcemia
Rapidly enlarging neck mass causing airway compromise

faq.a: No, MEN syndromes are inherited; however, sporadic tumours can mimic individual components.

faq.q: Is genetic testing required for diagnosis?
faq.a: It confirms the syndrome and guides family screening, but clinical criteria can diagnose when testing is unavailable.
Surgery is indicated for functional or malignant tumours; small non‑functioning lesions may be observed with close monitoring.

exam: List the three major MEN syndromes and their hallmark tumours.
Explain how you would screen a newly diagnosed MEN2 patient for pheochromocytoma before thyroid surgery.
Describe the management steps for a patient with MEN1 presenting with hypercalcemia and a gastrinoma.
